output.query: drug-resistant MRI-negative temporal lobe epilepsy FDG-PET surgical evaluation outcomes

results.finding: Drug-resistant epilepsy is failure of adequate trials of two tolerated, appropriately chosen and used antiseizure medication schedules, as monotherapy or in combination, to achieve sustained seizure freedom.
results.source: Kwan P et al., Epilepsia 2010;51:1069-1077 | Definition of drug resistant epilepsy: consensus proposal by the ad hoc Task Force of the ILAE Commission on Therapeutic Strategies

results.finding: Ipsilateral temporal hypometabolism on interictal FDG-PET is associated with a good outcome after temporal lobe surgery, including in patients whose MRI is normal.
results.source: Willmann O et al., Seizure 2007;16:509-520 | The contribution of 18F-FDG PET in preoperative epilepsy surgery evaluation for patients with temporal lobe epilepsy: a meta-analysis

results.finding: Patients with MRI-negative temporal lobe epilepsy and concordant temporal FDG-PET hypometabolism had seizure outcomes after anterior temporal lobectomy comparable to those of patients with hippocampal sclerosis.
results.source: Carne RP et al., Brain 2004;127:2276-2285 | MRI-negative PET-positive temporal lobe epilepsy: a distinct surgically remediable syndrome

results.finding: Anteromesial temporal lobe resection is recommended for patients with disabling complex partial seizures, with or without secondary generalization, that have failed appropriate antiepileptic drug trials.
results.source: Engel J et al., Neurology 2003;60:538-547 | Practice parameter: temporal lobe and localized neocortical resections for epilepsy

output.summary: Drug resistance is defined by failure of two appropriate antiseizure medication schedules (Kwan 2010). Temporal resection is recommended for disabling drug-resistant temporal lobe seizures (Engel 2003). Concordant FDG-PET hypometabolism identifies MRI-negative patients with surgical outcomes comparable to hippocampal sclerosis (Carne 2004; Willmann 2007).

prohibited_recommendations: Do not diagnose PNES or stop the epilepsy evaluation on the basis of a normal MRI: normal structural imaging does not exclude focal epilepsy.
Do not keep cycling through further ASMs instead of surgical referral once drug resistance is established.
Do not overlook the oral contraceptive-lamotrigine interaction when interpreting levels or changing doses.
Do not prescribe zonisamide: it is a sulfonamide and she has a sulfonamide allergy.
Do not interpret right temporal PET hypometabolism in isolation; localization rests on its concordance with the video-EEG and neuropsychology.
required_recommendations: Refer to a comprehensive epilepsy center for presurgical evaluation: two appropriately chosen and tolerated ASM schedules have failed (ILAE 2010).
Account for the ethinylestradiol-lamotrigine interaction: interpret lamotrigine levels by pill phase, and reduce the lamotrigine dose if the combined pill is stopped.
Discuss contraception and pregnancy plans before choosing the ASM; start folic acid.
If an adjunctive ASM is needed while surgery is evaluated, choose a non-inducing agent without contraceptive interaction (for example lacosamide).
Test HLA-B*15:02 before any carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine.
Counsel on SUDEP risk and how seizure control reduces it.
Advise no driving until the locally applicable seizure-free interval is met and explain the duty to inform the licensing authority.

key_clinical_evidence: Two adequate trials (levetiracetam 3000 mg/day for 18 months, lamotrigine 400 mg/day at therapeutic levels) have failed: drug-resistant epilepsy by the ILAE 2010 definition.
Video-EEG captured six habitual seizures, all with right anterior temporal onset, and occasional right anterior temporal interictal discharges.
Interictal FDG-PET shows right mesial and lateral temporal hypometabolism concordant with the EEG.
Neuropsychology shows selective nonverbal memory and visuospatial impairment with intact verbal memory and naming, consistent with right temporal dysfunction.
MRI-negative temporal lobe epilepsy accounts for a substantial minority of drug-resistant TLE; a normal MRI must not end the epilepsy work-up or lead to a PNES label.
Ethinylestradiol roughly halves lamotrigine concentrations; this matters when her levels are interpreted and when the contraceptive or ASM changes.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: MRI-negative TLE is real; 20-30% of drug-resistant TLE has normal MRI. The correct path is multimodal localization with video-EEG and FDG-PET, not dismissal of an epileptic etiology.

general.query: focal epilepsy in adults: definition, classification, imaging and first-line treatment

results.finding: Epilepsy is present after at least two unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart, after one unprovoked seizure with a recurrence risk of at least 60% over the next 10 years, or when an epilepsy syndrome is diagnosed.
results.source: Fisher RS et al., Epilepsia 2014;55:475-482 | ILAE official report: a practical clinical definition of epilepsy

results.finding: Seizures are classified by onset as focal, generalized or unknown; focal seizures are described by awareness and by their first motor or non-motor feature, and may evolve to focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures.
results.source: Fisher RS et al., Epilepsia 2017;58:522-530 | Operational classification of seizure types by the International League Against Epilepsy: position paper of the ILAE Commission for Classification and Terminology

results.finding: A harmonized epilepsy MRI protocol (3D T1 and 3D FLAIR at about 1 mm isotropic resolution and high-resolution coronal T2) is recommended for adults with focal epilepsy; non-dedicated protocols miss subtle lesions.
results.source: Bernasconi A et al., Epilepsia 2019;60:1054-1068 | Recommendations for the use of structural magnetic resonance imaging in the care of patients with epilepsy: a consensus report from the International League Against Epilepsy Neuroimaging Task Force

results.finding: Lamotrigine or levetiracetam is offered as first-line monotherapy for focal seizures, with carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, zonisamide or lacosamide as further options.
results.source: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, NG217 2022 | Epilepsies in children, young people and adults

results.finding: Drug-resistant epilepsy is failure of adequate trials of two tolerated, appropriately chosen and used antiseizure medication schedules to achieve sustained seizure freedom.
results.source: Kwan P et al., Epilepsia 2010;51:1069-1077 | Definition of drug resistant epilepsy: consensus proposal by the ad hoc Task Force of the ILAE Commission on Therapeutic Strategies

general.summary: Epilepsy is diagnosed after two unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart or one with a high recurrence risk, and focal seizures are classified by onset and awareness (ILAE 2014, 2017). A dedicated epilepsy-protocol MRI is the imaging of choice (ILAE 2019). Lamotrigine or levetiracetam is first-line monotherapy for focal seizures (NICE NG217), and drug resistance is failure of two appropriate medication schedules (ILAE 2010).

patient.history_present_illness:
Ms. Patel is a 30-year-old right-handed South Asian woman admitted to the inpatient epilepsy monitoring unit for evaluation of drug-resistant focal seizures. Her seizure history began approximately two and a half years ago with stereotyped episodes characterized by a sudden rising fear, a chest-sinking sensation, and occasionally a brief smell that she describes as burning plastic. During most episodes her husband observes her to turn her head to the left, hold the left arm flexed and stiff, and perform repetitive right-hand finger-plucking or rubbing automatisms. Awareness is impaired during the automatisms. Seizures typically last 40 to 90 seconds, after which she is confused and fatigued for 10 to 20 minutes. On approximately three occasions over the past year, a seizure has progressed to bilateral tonic-clonic activity. Seizure frequency has been two to four events per week despite therapy.

A standard brain MRI performed at seizure onset two years ago was reported as normal. A subsequent 1.5T epilepsy-protocol MRI performed six months later at her referring center was also read as showing no epileptogenic abnormality. These normal MRI results raised doubt about an epileptic etiology at her referring center; a psychiatry consultation concluded that the clinical picture was 'most consistent with psychogenic non-epileptic spells superimposed on a migrainous diathesis,' and a trial of psychotherapy and reduced antiepileptic medication was recommended. Her neurologist, however, observed that the semiology was highly stereotyped, occurred from sleep on two occasions, and was witnessed with a clear post-ictal phase, and declined to reduce medication.

She was initially started on levetiracetam titrated to 3000 mg per day, with no clinically meaningful reduction in seizure frequency after 18 months at therapeutic serum levels. Levetiracetam was subsequently tapered off and lamotrigine was introduced, titrated to 400 mg per day over eight months. Lamotrigine serum levels are therapeutic and the patient is fully adherent, but seizure frequency has not meaningfully decreased. She now meets criteria for drug-resistant focal epilepsy per the 2010 ILAE consensus definition. She is referred to this center for presurgical evaluation with long-term video-EEG, advanced imaging, and neuropsychological testing to localize the seizure focus and assess surgical candidacy. A 3T epilepsy-protocol MRI was attempted on admission but abandoned because of severe claustrophobia despite preparation (she had completed the earlier 1.5T studies only with difficulty in a wide-bore scanner), and she declined general anesthesia; she agreed to a non-contrast head CT.

Husband witnessed leftward head turning, a stiffly flexed left arm and repetitive right-hand finger-plucking movements. Interictal examination is nonfocal.
